title: Esther 2:1–7
context: After the wrath of Ahasuerus is pacified, he remembers Vashti and what was decreed against her. The king’s servants propose a search for beautiful young virgins, to be gathered to the citadel of Susa under Hegai, keeper of the women, so that the maiden who pleases the king may be queen instead of Vashti. The proposal pleases the king. The narrative then introduces Mordecai, a Jew in Susa, “the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite,” and says that he, or a named ancestor, “had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captives who had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah.” Whether that exile clause refers to Mordecai himself or to Kish is not certain and should be left open. Some readers also compare this Kish, a Benjamite, with Saul’s father in 1 Samuel 9; the names invite the comparison, but the identification is not stated here and should be hedged. The Agagite conflict still lies ahead in chapter 3 and need not be developed in this unit. Mordecai has brought up Hadassah, that is Esther, his uncle’s daughter, an orphan, as his own daughter. The gathering of the young women should be told soberly, as an imperial search, without prurience and without modern culture-war framing. The book still does not name God. Hidden-providence readings of Esther’s place in this search are common in both traditions and remain shared and hedged. Both traditions take the unit as the introduction of the two figures who will carry the story, without a contrast over the genealogy.

verses.text: After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was pacified, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her.
verses.arminianNotes:
“After these things, when the wrath of King Ahasuerus was pacified, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her.” The anger of 1:12 has cooled, and memory returns, both of the queen’s deed and of the irreversible decree. The verse does not say that he regrets the law in so many words, and no change of heart the text leaves unstated is invented.

Arminian readers take the pacified wrath and the remembrance as a real turn in the king, a human mood on which the next proposal will play.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a court after anger: Vashti is remembered, and so is the decree, the two held together as the situation the servants will now address.

Both traditions keep the line as narrative aftermath, not as a decoded sign, and they invent no contrast over the king’s feelings.

verses.text: Then the king’s servants who served him said, “Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king’s servants say, “Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king.” The search is their proposal, not yet a law, and it is stated in the blunt terms of the court: beauty is what is to be sought. The line should be read soberly, as the opening of an imperial gathering, not as a scene to be embellished.

Arminian readers take the servants’ counsel as a real court suggestion, a human plan that will gather many young women, including, later, Esther.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also leave the proposal in the servants’ mouths. The king is advised to seek beautiful young virgins, the practical sequel to an emptied royal estate.

Both traditions handle the search without prurience and without a modern culture-war frame, and they invent no contrast over the advice.

verses.text: Let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the beautiful young virgins to the citadel of Susa, to the women’s house, to the custody of Hegai the king’s eunuch, keeper of the women. Let cosmetics be given them;
verses.arminianNotes:
Officers are to be appointed in all the provinces to “gather together all the beautiful young virgins to the citadel of Susa, to the women’s house, to the custody of Hegai the king’s eunuch, keeper of the women.” Cosmetics are to be given them. The gathering is empire-wide, and the young women are placed in custody in the women’s house. The notes report that arrangement as the text describes it, without softening it into a merely voluntary pageant or hardening it into a later slogan.

Arminian readers take the roundup as a real royal order, many lives moved by a court decision they did not make, the setting in which Esther will later be taken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep Hegai, the women’s house, and the cosmetics as the narrative’s own account of how the candidates were collected and prepared.

Both traditions tell the gathering soberly and refuse to use the verse as a culture-war example.

verses.text: and let the maiden who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti.” The thing pleased the king, and he did so.
verses.arminianNotes:
The aim is stated: “let the maiden who pleases the king be queen instead of Vashti.” The thing pleases the king, and he does so. The vacancy Memucan created is now to be filled by a new queen chosen in this way. The book still does not name God; a providence reading of the opening is common in both traditions and should be held as a reading of the story’s shape, not as a hidden word in the servants’ plan.

Arminian readers take the king’s consent as a real decision, the search now under way by his will.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear the plan approved and begun, the phrase “instead of Vashti” tying this chapter to the decree of chapter 1.

Both traditions keep hidden-providence readings shared and hedged, and they invent no contrast over the king’s pleasure in the plan.

verses.text: There was a certain Jew in the citadel of Susa whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite,
verses.arminianNotes:
There was “a certain Jew in the citadel of Susa whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite”. Mordecai is introduced by people, city, and line. The names Jair, Shimei, and Kish, and the tribe of Benjamin, lead some readers to compare this Kish with Saul’s father in 1 Samuel 9:1, already drafted in this worktree. The comparison is natural and may be named; it is not stated in this verse and should be hedged, not treated as a settled identification. The later Agagite conflict of chapter 3 is not yet in view and need not be developed here.

Arminian readers take Mordecai as a real Jew of Benjamin in Susa, named by a family line, without forcing the Kish of 1 Samuel 9 into the verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the genealogy as the text gives it, a Benjamite line ending in Kish, and they leave the link with Saul’s father as a possible, unproved connection.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the names, and they do not settle the ancestry beyond what is written.

verses.text: who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captives who had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.
verses.arminianNotes:
The next clause says, “who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captives who had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away.” The relative “who” may attach to Mordecai, or to Kish, the last ancestor named in 2:5. If it names Mordecai himself, he would be a survivor of Jeconiah’s exile; if it names Kish, the exile is placed a generation or more earlier in the family. Both readings have been offered, and the grammar does not settle the question. The notes leave it open, without forcing a chronology from a later identification of Ahasuerus.

Arminian readers report both attachments of the clause and refuse to decide the age or generation of Mordecai as if the verse had made it plain.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hedge the point. The exile with Jeconiah, known from 2 Kings 24 and 2 Chronicles 36, is a real event in the family’s past; whether Mordecai or Kish is the one carried away remains an open question.

Both traditions invent no contrast over the grammar, and they do not build a history the clause does not fix.

verses.text: He brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter; for she had neither father nor mother. The maiden was fair and beautiful; and when her father and mother were dead, Mordecai took her for his own daughter.
verses.arminianNotes:
Mordecai “brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter; for she had neither father nor mother.” She is fair and beautiful, and when her parents were dead he took her for his own daughter. Hadassah is given as her name, Esther as the name by which she is also known. She is his cousin, an orphan in his house. The verse states her beauty because the search has already been described; it is not lingered on here.

Arminian readers take the adoption as a real family care, Mordecai raising his uncle’s daughter as his own, the relationship that will govern her later obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a named orphan, Hadassah called Esther, taken as a daughter, the household in which her people and her future will first be hidden and then, later, revealed.

Both traditions introduce her soberly, without a contrast over the two names, and without turning the orphan notice into a symbol.
